intro.t: The shortest Gospel, probably the first written, moving fast to the cross.
b: Mark tells the story of Jesus at speed. ‘Immediately’ is one of his favourite words, and there is no birth story and almost no long teaching. He shows Jesus acting with God’s authority over sickness, demons, nature, sin and death, and yet constantly misunderstood, even by his own disciples.

The Gospel turns on a question at its centre: ‘Who do you say I am?’ (8:29). Peter answers, ‘You are the Christ.’ From then on Jesus explains what kind of Christ he is: ‘the Son of Man must suffer’ (8:31), and he ‘did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many’ (10:45). Almost a third of the book covers his last week. The first human being in Mark to call Jesus ‘the Son of God’ is a Roman centurion watching him die (15:39).

What the early church said. The Gospel does not name its author, but every early witness gives the same answer. Papias, a bishop in Asia Minor writing early in the 2nd century and quoted by Eusebius, passed on what ‘the elder’ had told him: ‘Mark, having become the interpreter of Peter, wrote down accurately, though not in order, whatsoever he remembered of the things said or done by Christ.’ Irenaeus (about AD 180) writes of Peter and Paul: ‘After their departure, Mark, the disciple and interpreter of Peter, did also hand down to us in writing what had been preached by Peter.’ The anti-Marcionite prologue adds that Mark wrote in Italy.

Where scholars stand. Every surviving manuscript carries the title ‘According to Mark’; Martin Hengel and Richard Bauckham argue that the titles go back to the first copies. The Lexham Bible Dictionary estimates that about 60 percent of scholars accept that John Mark wrote it; the rest regard the author as unknown, usually because they doubt Papias.

The case for Mark. If the church had been inventing an author, it would hardly have chosen Mark. He was not an apostle. He was the young man who abandoned Paul and Barnabas on their first journey (Acts 13:13; 15:37–39), though later Paul called him ‘useful to me for the ministry’ (2 Timothy 4:11). Peter calls him ‘my son Mark’ in a letter from ‘Babylon’, probably Rome (1 Peter 5:13). The Gospel itself fits Papias’s description: vivid, eyewitness-like detail, Peter prominent and his failures told plainly, and an outline that matches Peter’s preaching in Acts 10:36–43, from John’s baptism to the resurrection.

b: Rome, for Gentile believers (Widely accepted). Mark explains Jewish customs (7:3–4), translates Aramaic words (5:41; 7:34; 15:34), and uses Latin terms written in Greek letters, such as legion, denarius and praetorium. It mentions Rufus (15:21), perhaps the Rufus greeted in Romans 16:13. Christians in Rome suffered terribly under Nero after the fire of AD 64; Tacitus and 1 Clement describe it. A Gospel that spends so much time on suffering, betrayal and faithfulness under trial would speak directly to them. Some scholars suggest Syria or Galilee instead.

Date (Debated). Those who accept the tradition date it shortly after Peter’s death, about AD 65–70. Most think it was written before the temple was destroyed in AD 70, since Mark does not describe the event. A few date it soon after 70, reading 13:14 as a reference to it. Others, following J. A. T. Robinson, date it earlier still, in the 50s, because Luke and Acts seem to be written before 70 and Luke used Mark.

hist.t: Matthew, Mark and Luke: who used whom? (the ‘Synoptic problem’)
b: Matthew, Mark and Luke tell many of the same stories, often in the same order and with the same wording; they are called the ‘Synoptic’ Gospels (Greek: ‘seen together’). Of Mark’s 661 verses, about 606 have a parallel in Matthew and about 380 in Luke; only some 31 verses of Mark have no parallel in either.

Mark first (Widely accepted). Since the 19th century most scholars have concluded that Mark was written first and that Matthew and Luke each used it, smoothing its rough Greek and adding their own material. The material Matthew and Luke share but Mark lacks (about 200–250 verses, mostly sayings of Jesus) is usually explained by a lost collection of sayings called ‘Q’ (from German Quelle, ‘source’). Some suggest Papias’s remark that Matthew compiled ‘the oracles’ refers to something like it.

Other views (Debated). Augustine thought Mark had abridged Matthew, and many Catholic scholars long defended Matthew’s priority; a minority still argue that Matthew came first, or that Luke used Matthew directly with no need for Q. No copy of Q has ever been found.

None of these theories requires that the Gospel writers were careless or untrustworthy. Luke openly says he used earlier accounts and eyewitness testimony (Luke 1:1–4). Using written sources was normal and responsible history-writing.

b: The Jewish historian Josephus (about AD 37–100) mentions Jesus twice. In Antiquities 20.200 he records the stoning of ‘the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James’. Almost all scholars accept this passage as genuine.

In Antiquities 18.63–64 our copies call Jesus ‘a wise man’ and ‘a doer of wonderful works’, and say Pilate condemned him to the cross. But they also contain phrases a non-Christian Jew is unlikely to have written (for example ‘He was the Christ’). Many scholars therefore think Josephus wrote a shorter, neutral passage about Jesus and that Christian copyists later added to it. Others think the whole passage is a later insertion; a few defend it as it stands. Either way, the passage on James shows that Josephus knew of Jesus.

1.h: The first line is the thesis
1.t: Mark does not open with a genealogy or a nativity but with a claim. “Beginning” deliberately echoes the first words of Genesis: something is starting here on that scale. “Gospel” was not yet a religious word — in the Roman world it announced an imperial victory or the birth of an emperor. To attach it to an executed Galilean is a political provocation as much as a theological one. Note the footnote: some early manuscripts lack “the Son of God”, though the phrase reappears at the centre and the climax of the book regardless.

1.h: All three persons at the Jordan
1.t: The Son is baptised, the Spirit descends, the Father speaks. The Trinity is not a doctrine developed centuries later and read backwards into the text; it is simply what is happening in this scene. The Father’s words splice Psalm 2:7, spoken to the messianic king, with Isaiah 42:1, spoken to the suffering Servant. Both identities are assigned before Jesus has done anything, and the tension between them drives the rest of the Gospel.

Mark gives the temptation two verses where Matthew and Luke give forty. The verb is violent — the Spirit throws him out into the wilderness. Israel spent forty years in the wilderness and failed; Jesus spends forty days and does not. The wild animals are Mark’s detail alone, and may hint at Eden restored.

Nothing is said about why they follow. Mark is not interested in their psychology but in his authority: he speaks, and men leave their livelihood mid-shift. Zebedee is left in the boat with the hired men, which tells you this was a business of some size. Following costs something real from the first sentence.

The crowd’s reaction is that he teaches with authority, “not as the scribes”. A scribe’s authority was derivative — he cited those before him. Jesus cites nobody. The demon, notably, is the first character in the Gospel to identify him correctly, and is immediately silenced. Throughout Mark the supernatural realm knows exactly who he is while the human characters do not.

Under the law, touching a leper made you unclean. Jesus touches him and the man is cleansed instead. The direction of contagion reverses. This is a small picture of the whole gospel: holiness that goes out and absorbs rather than holiness that withdraws and protects itself.

2.t: The scribes’ reasoning is impeccable: only God forgives sins, therefore this is blasphemy. Their logic is right and their conclusion is wrong, and the only way out is the one they will not take. Jesus does not soften the claim; he proves it with something visible. “Son of Man” here is not a modest self-description — it is drawn from Daniel 7:13–14, where a human figure approaches the Ancient of Days and receives everlasting dominion.

Levi collected tax for Rome from his own people, which made him a collaborator as well as a thief. Table fellowship in this culture signalled acceptance, which is precisely why the objection is raised. Jesus’ reply is not that these people are fine as they are — he calls them sick and himself the doctor. Both halves of that matter.

2.h: Not a patch on the old
2.t: The new wine imagery is often softened into a general point about change. Its actual force is sharper: what Jesus brings cannot be contained inside the existing structures of Second Temple religion. Something is being replaced, not renovated.

3.h: The alliance that should not exist
3.t: Pharisees were religious separatists; Herodians were political collaborators with Rome. They agreed on almost nothing except, now, this. Mark places the decision to kill Jesus in chapter three of sixteen — the outcome is fixed before a third of the book has passed, and everything after moves toward it.

The number is the point. Twelve tribes, twelve apostles: Jesus is constituting a renewed Israel around himself. Judas is named in the list from the beginning, with his end already attached, which Mark does without comment.

This passage has caused more unnecessary fear than almost any other. What Jesus condemns is the settled, deliberate attribution of the Holy Spirit’s work to Satan — looking at undeniable good and calling it evil in order to avoid its implications. It is a hardened position, not a moment of doubt or a blasphemous thought that intruded. The pastoral point follows logically: anyone anxious about having committed it has demonstrated by that anxiety that they have not. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

Mark sandwiches the Beelzebul controversy inside the story of Jesus’ family coming to seize him because they think he is out of his mind. The structure is intentional. Both his relatives and the religious authorities conclude something is wrong with him; the difference is only in what they blame.

4.t: The parable is not primarily about identifying which soil you are. It is an explanation of why the ministry is producing such mixed results, and a promise that despite the waste the harvest will be absurdly large. Thirty, sixty and a hundredfold were extraordinary yields in first-century Palestine, where sevenfold was a good year.

4.h: The hardest verses in the chapter
4.t: Jesus quotes Isaiah 6:9–10 to explain that parables both reveal and conceal. This sits uncomfortably with modern assumptions, and it should. The point is that hearing is not a neutral capacity everyone possesses and some choose to use; genuine understanding is given. Those already resisting find that the parables harden the resistance. This is why the disciples’ access to explanation is a gift rather than a reward — they understand no better than anyone else, as the next four chapters repeatedly show. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

In the Old Testament, stilling the sea is something God does and nobody else — Psalm 107:29 is the closest parallel and the disciples would have known it. Their terror after the calm is greater than their terror during the storm, and rightly so. The question they ask is Mark’s question, and he will not answer it plainly until chapter 8.

5.t: A Roman legion was roughly six thousand men, and the name is unlikely to be accidental in a Gospel written for readers under Roman power. The setting is Gentile territory — hence the pigs — and the healed man becomes the first person commissioned to tell rather than to keep silent. Outside Israel, the misunderstanding that the secret protects against does not apply.

Mark sandwiches the bleeding woman inside Jairus’s story, and the two are linked by the number twelve — she has bled for twelve years, the girl is twelve years old. Both are ritually unclean situations; both are reversed by touch. Jairus has to stand and wait while his daughter dies, which is Mark’s honest acknowledgement that delay is part of the experience even when the outcome is good.
Mark preserves the actual words — talitha koum — and then translates them. He does this several times. It is the kind of detail that survives when a story comes from someone who was in the room.

6.t: Mark says plainly that Jesus could do no miracle there beyond a few healings, and that he marvelled at their unbelief. This is not a statement about a shortage of divine power; it is a statement about the nature of what he came to do. Miracles in Mark are never displays for their own sake — they meet faith, and where there is none they have nothing to meet.

The execution of John is the single passage in Mark where Jesus does not appear, and it is told in unusual detail. Its placement, between the sending of the Twelve and their return, is a warning shot: this is what happens to those who speak for God to people in power. Mark’s first readers, under Nero, would not have missed it.

“Sheep without a shepherd” is a quotation, not a sentiment — it comes from Numbers 27:17 and is picked up in Ezekiel 34, where God condemns Israel’s leaders and promises to shepherd the flock himself. Sitting them down on green grass points at Psalm 23. Mark is telling you who is doing the feeding.

6.h: He meant to pass by them
6.t: An odd detail until you notice where it comes from. In Exodus 33 and 1 Kings 19, God “passes by” Moses and Elijah — it is the technical language of a divine appearance. Combined with the words rendered “It is I”, which in Greek are simply “I am”, this is a theophany on the water. Mark closes by noting the disciples’ hearts were hardened, using the same word he applies to the Pharisees.

7.t: The specific abuse is declaring property dedicated to the temple so that it becomes unavailable to support ageing parents, while the declarer retains its use. Jesus’ charge is not that tradition is worthless but that this tradition is being used to cancel a commandment. The principle generalises uncomfortably well.

The clause declaring all foods clean is Mark’s editorial note, not part of Jesus’ speech. It is a remarkable thing for a first-century Jewish writer to say, and it indicates how far the implications had been worked out by the time he wrote. The food laws that separated Israel from the nations are over.

7.h: The only person who wins an argument
7.t: Jesus’ words to the Syrophoenician woman are deliberately hard, and attempts to soften them usually make the passage worse. She does not dispute the priority he states — she accepts it and presses for the overflow. She is the only character in the Gospels who takes Jesus’ own image and turns it, and he commends her for exactly that. Immediately afterwards he feeds a Gentile crowd.

8.t: Two feedings have happened and the disciples worry about bread. Jesus’ questions here — do you have eyes and fail to see, ears and fail to hear — apply to the disciples the same language chapter 4 applied to outsiders. The gap between them and the crowd is smaller than they think.

The only miracle in the Gospels that takes two attempts, and it is placed here deliberately. The man first sees people looking like walking trees, then sees clearly. In the very next scene Peter identifies Jesus correctly and then immediately misunderstands what it means. The healing is a deliberate commentary on the confession that follows.

Caesarea Philippi was a centre of pagan worship, which makes it a pointed place to ask the question. Peter’s answer is right, and Jesus orders silence. This is the midpoint of the book; from here the geography turns toward Jerusalem and the subject turns to the cross.

Peter is rebuked in the strongest terms in the Gospel, moments after being right. The rebuke is not for doubting that Jesus is Messiah but for assuming he knows what a Messiah does. Note the word “must” in the prediction — the cross is not a tragic accident that befalls the plan; it is the plan.

9.t: Moses and Elijah represent the law and the prophets; their presence and then their disappearance, leaving Jesus alone, is the point of the scene. The Father’s command echoes Deuteronomy 18:15, the promise of a prophet like Moses to whom Israel must listen. Peter’s instinct to build shelters is an attempt to make a permanent arrangement of a moment that was never meant to be one.

9.h: The most honest prayer in the Bible
9.t: “I believe; help my unbelief” is a contradiction, and it is answered anyway. It is worth noticing what Jesus does not do: he does not tell the man to come back when he is more certain. Faith that is mixed with doubt is still faith, and it is still enough. Most Christians will pray this sentence at some point, and they are in good company.

The second passion prediction is followed immediately by the disciples debating which of them is greatest. Mark reports this without editorial comment, which is its own comment. Jesus’ answer places a child — a person of no status whatever in that society — at the centre of the room.

10.t: Asked to take a side in a rabbinic dispute about grounds for divorce, Jesus goes past the Mosaic concession to Genesis. The permission existed, he says, because of hardness of heart — a regulation of failure rather than a statement of intent. He treats the creation account as normative and as historical, which is worth noting on its own.

10.h: Jesus looked at him and loved him
10.t: Mark alone records the look and the love, which changes the tone of everything that follows. The demand is not a general requirement laid on all disciples but a diagnosis of this man’s particular idol, aimed precisely. The disciples’ astonishment reflects an assumption that wealth signalled God’s favour. Jesus’ answer — that it is impossible for anyone, and possible only with God — is as clear a statement of salvation by grace as the Gospels contain.

The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. “Ransom” is a marketplace and slave-market word: a price paid to secure release. “For many” echoes Isaiah 53:11–12 and the Servant who bears the sins of many. Every major strand of the New Testament’s understanding of the cross is already present in this one sentence, spoken by Jesus about himself.

Bartimaeus is the only person healed in Mark whose name is recorded. He addresses Jesus as Son of David — a messianic title — and is not silenced, because Jerusalem is now in view. Mark ends the account by saying he followed Jesus on the road, and the road leads directly to the cross. He is the model disciple, and he is a blind beggar.

11.t: The arrangements are too specific to be spontaneous. Jesus is staging Zechariah 9:9 — a king coming humble and riding on a donkey, the animal of peace rather than the warhorse. The crowd’s shout comes from Psalm 118. They are expecting a different kind of king from the one they have.

11.h: The fig tree and the temple
11.t: Mark splits the fig tree around the temple cleansing, which is the clearest example of his sandwiching technique. The tree is in leaf but bears nothing; the temple is in operation but produces nothing. One interprets the other. The quotation about a house of prayer for all nations comes from Isaiah 56:7, and the trading was taking place in the only court Gentiles were permitted to enter.

Jesus' promises about prayer are real and bold, but they sit inside the rest of Scripture, where Jesus himself asked for the cup to pass and was not spared, and Paul's thorn was not removed. The historic Christian understanding is that God always hears and always answers in love, sometimes by giving what we ask, sometimes by giving something better, and sometimes by giving himself in the waiting. Unanswered prayer is not usually evidence of weak faith; it is one of the ordinary experiences of every believer in Scripture. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

12.t: The vineyard is Isaiah 5, and the audience recognised it immediately — Mark tells us they knew the parable was about them. The escalation from servants to the beloved son is the whole history of Israel’s prophets, and Jesus places himself at the end of it in a category of his own.

The trap is real: say yes and lose the crowd, say no and face Rome. Jesus’ answer is not a tidy separation of religion and politics. The coin bears Caesar’s image so return it to him — and you bear God’s image, so the question of what is owed to God answers itself and is not a small one.

Usually read as a lesson in generosity, and it is. But notice its placement, directly after Jesus condemns scribes who devour widows’ houses and immediately before he predicts the temple’s destruction. The woman gives everything to an institution that is about to fall and that has been exploiting people like her. The admiration and the lament are held together.

13.t: Herod’s temple was one of the wonders of the ancient world and some of its foundation stones weighed over fifty tonnes. The prediction was literally fulfilled in AD 70, within the lifetime of many who heard it.

The discourse moves between the fall of Jerusalem and the final return, and interpreters divide over where the line falls. The most defensible reading takes the detailed warnings about Judea as concerning AD 70, and the cosmic language from verse 24 as concerning the end. Whatever the division, the repeated instruction is not to calculate but to stay awake — and Jesus states plainly that the day is not known even to the Son. Worth talking through with a pastor or a mature Christian you trust.

14.h: She has done what she could
14.t: The perfume was worth close to a year’s wages. The objection about the poor is reasonable, and Jesus does not dismiss it so much as subordinate it to the moment. Sandwiched between Judas’s betrayal arrangements on either side, the contrast is stark: one person pours out everything, another sells him for silver.

“This is my body” is said while his body is visibly present, which should govern how literally the words are taken. The covenant language comes from Exodus 24 and Jeremiah 31. Christians have divided for centuries over what happens at the table; what is not in dispute is that his death is being interpreted, by him, in advance, as a sacrifice that establishes a covenant.

Mark preserves the Aramaic word for Father, the ordinary family word. The prayer asks for the cup to pass and then submits, and both halves are recorded. This is the clearest window in the Gospels into the genuine humanity of Jesus — not a performance of distress but distress. That he asks and is not spared says something important about what unanswered prayer can mean.

Asked directly whether he is the Messiah, the Son of the Blessed One, Jesus answers with two words that in Greek are simply “I am”, and then combines Daniel 7 with Psalm 110. He claims divine identity, enthronement and the role of coming judge in one sentence. The high priest’s reaction shows the claim was understood exactly as intended.

If this Gospel carries Peter’s testimony, then the most humiliating account of Peter in the New Testament comes from Peter. Mark records no rehabilitation scene; the only forward-looking word is the message at the tomb that names Peter specifically.

15.t: Jesus quotes the opening line of Psalm 22, in Aramaic. Two things are true at once and both matter. He is genuinely bearing abandonment, and he is reaching for Scripture to say so — and Psalm 22, which begins in that darkness, ends in vindication and worldwide worship. The quotation is not despair with no floor under it.
The curtain separated the Most Holy Place from everything else and enforced the distance between God and people. Mark specifies the direction of the tear. This is not something achieved from below.

Mark’s whole argument lands here. The first human being in the Gospel to confess Jesus as Son of God is a Roman officer who has just supervised his execution, and what convinces him is not a miracle but the manner of the death. This closes the frame opened in 1:1 — and the fact that it is a Gentile who sees it first would not have been lost on Mark’s readers in Rome.

16.h: An ending that does not feel like one
16.t: The women are told that he is risen and that the disciples — and Peter by name — will see him. Then they flee and say nothing, and the Greek text ends on a conjunction, mid-breath. Many readers have found this unsatisfying; it may be exactly the point. The one group in the Gospel who obey and speak are the readers, and Mark has left the last move to them.

Most modern Bibles mark this passage off, and the BSB is no exception. The two earliest and most reliable complete manuscripts of Mark end at verse 8, as do several early translations and patristic witnesses; the longer ending uses vocabulary and style found nowhere else in Mark. Some manuscripts carry a shorter alternative ending instead. None of this is hidden or recent — translators flag it precisely because the evidence is public, and no Christian doctrine depends on these verses. It is a good example of textual criticism working as it should.

1.h: The Mission of John the Baptist
1.ctx: Mark starts not with Jesus’ birth but with his public ministry, about AD 28–30. The Old Testament had closed with a promise that God would send a messenger, Elijah, to prepare his way (Malachi 3:1; 4:5).
1.mean: ‘This is the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.’ Mark joins two prophecies (Malachi 3:1 and Isaiah 40:3) under the name of the greater prophet, Isaiah: God will send a messenger ahead to ‘Prepare the way for the Lord’. That messenger is John. He appears in the wilderness, ‘preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins’, and crowds come from all Judea and Jerusalem, confessing their sins. His camel’s hair and leather belt deliberately recall Elijah (2 Kings 1:8). He points away from himself: ‘After me will come One more powerful than I’, whose sandals he is not worthy to untie, a slave’s job. ‘I baptize you with water, but He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.’ Then Jesus comes from Nazareth and is baptised. As he comes up, he sees the heavens ‘breaking open’ and the Spirit descending like a dove, and the Father says: ‘You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased.’
1.big: The Father, the Son and the Spirit all appear at the start of the gospel, and the ‘Lord’ whose way Isaiah said would be prepared turns out to be Jesus.
1.diff: Why was Jesus baptised? John’s was a baptism of repentance, and Jesus had nothing to repent of. Christians have answered that he was identifying himself with the sinners he came to save, and (as Matthew 3:15 puts it) fulfilling ‘all righteousness’. Calvin: Jesus was baptised ‘that he might render full obedience to the Father’, and ‘that he might consecrate baptism in his own body, that we might have it in common with him’. A textual note: some early manuscripts lack ‘the Son of God’ in verse 1 (BSB footnote), but the title is central to Mark either way (1:11; 15:39).

b: John is one of the few people in the Gospels also described by a Jewish historian of the time. Josephus calls him ‘John, that was called the Baptist’, ‘a good man’ who urged the Jews to practise righteousness towards one another and piety towards God, and so to come to baptism. Crowds flocked to him, and Herod Antipas, fearing an uprising, had him imprisoned and executed (see 6:14–29).

Josephus explains John’s baptism differently from Mark: as a purification of the body for those whose souls were already cleansed by righteousness. Mark says it was ‘for the forgiveness of sins’. Josephus was writing for Roman readers and may have recast John in terms they would understand.

John and Qumran (Debated). John preached in the Judean wilderness near the Jordan, not far from Qumran, where the Dead Sea Scrolls were found. The Qumran community also applied Isaiah 40:3 to itself and practised ritual washings. Some scholars think John may once have been connected with it; others see only a shared Jewish background. There is no direct evidence either way.

1.h: The Temptation and Preaching of Jesus
1.ctx: ‘Forty days’ in the wilderness recalls Israel’s forty years there, and Moses’ and Elijah’s forty days (Exodus 34:28; 1 Kings 19:8).
1.mean: ‘At once the Spirit drove Jesus into the wilderness’, where he was tempted by Satan for forty days. Mark gives only three details: Satan, ‘the wild animals’, and ‘the angels ministered to Him’. Where Israel failed in the wilderness, the Son is tested and stands. Mark’s Roman readers, some facing wild beasts in the arena, may have noticed that Jesus had been among the beasts and was kept. ‘After the arrest of John’ Jesus goes into Galilee with his message: ‘The time is fulfilled,’ he said, ‘and the kingdom of God is near. Repent and believe in the gospel!’
1.big: The long-awaited reign of God has arrived in Jesus, and the right response is to turn round and trust the good news.
1.diff: Repent and believe. All Christians agree that both are needed. Reformed theology holds that both are gifts that follow from God’s regenerating work in the heart (Westminster Confession 10). Arminian (Wesleyan) theology holds that God’s prevenient grace enables every hearer to respond, and that people can resist it. Catholic and Orthodox teaching also stresses grace going first, with human freedom cooperating. The command is the same in every tradition.

1.ctx: Fishing was a major industry on the Sea of Galilee (a freshwater lake about 21 km by 13 km). Zebedee had a boat and hired men, so this was a family business of some size.
1.mean: Walking by the lake, Jesus sees Simon and Andrew casting a net. ‘Come, follow Me,’ he says, ‘and I will make you fishers of men.’ ‘And at once they left their nets and followed Him.’ Further on he calls James and John, who leave their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men. Jewish students normally chose a rabbi to follow; here the teacher chooses and calls. They leave work, family and security on his word alone.
1.big: Following Jesus starts with his call, and it costs something real.

hist.t: A fishing boat from Jesus’ time
b: In 1986, during a drought that lowered the Sea of Galilee, two members of Kibbutz Ginosar found the remains of an ancient wooden boat in the mud of the shore. An Israeli team led by the nautical archaeologist Shelley Wachsmann excavated it. It is about 8 m (26 feet) long, built mainly of cedar and oak and much repaired. Radiocarbon dating places it around the 1st century BC to the 1st century AD.

It is often called ‘the Jesus boat’, but there is no evidence connecting it with Jesus or his disciples. What it does show is the kind of boat Galilean fishermen used in their day, large enough to carry a crew and passengers, like the boat in which Jesus slept during the storm (4:35–41). It is displayed at Kibbutz Ginosar.

1.ctx: Synagogue services included readings from the Law and the Prophets and could include teaching by a visiting teacher. The scribes were experts in the Law, who taught by citing earlier authorities.
1.mean: In the Capernaum synagogue people are ‘astonished at His teaching, because He taught as one who had authority, and not as the scribes’. Then a man with an unclean spirit cries out: ‘What do You want with us, Jesus of Nazareth? Have You come to destroy us? I know who You are—the Holy One of God!’ Jesus silences it and commands it out, and it leaves with a shriek. The crowd sees the connection: ‘A new teaching with authority! He commands even the unclean spirits, and they obey Him!’ His word does what it says.
1.big: Jesus’ authority is not borrowed from earlier teachers; evil itself recognises and obeys him.
1.diff: Demons and modern readers. Some modern readers explain the Gospels’ demons as ancient descriptions of mental or physical illness. The Gospels themselves distinguish possession from sickness (1:34), and the historic churches of every tradition hold that evil spirits are real personal beings. Calvin called the view that devils are ‘merely the depraved affections of men’ the ‘foolish trifling’ of irreligious men. Christians also agree that not every illness is demonic, and that medicine is God’s good gift.

b: Capernaum, on the north-west shore of the Sea of Galilee, was a small fishing town on the road to Damascus, with a tax post (compare Mark 2:14). A Roman milestone was found near the synagogue. The white limestone synagogue visitors see today dates from the 4th or 5th century AD (about 10,000 coins were found beneath its floor), but it stands on the foundations of an earlier one, probably the synagogue of Jesus’ day (compare Luke 7:5).

Just south of it is an octagonal church built over the walls of an earlier house. The excavators believe this was Peter’s house (Mark 1:29), venerated by Christians from early times; Italian archaeologists report the name Peter among graffiti scratched on its walls. The identification is reasonable but cannot be proved.

1.ctx: The Sabbath ended at sunset. Carrying the sick through the town before then would have counted as work, which is why the crowds wait until ‘after sunset’.
1.mean: Leaving the synagogue they go to Simon and Andrew’s home. Simon’s mother-in-law is in bed with a fever. Jesus takes her by the hand and helps her up; the fever leaves and ‘she began to serve them’. That evening ‘the whole town gathered at the door’, and he heals many and drives out many demons, ‘But He would not allow the demons to speak, because they knew who He was.’
1.big: Jesus brings God’s healing right into an ordinary home, and the healed woman responds by serving.
1.diff: Peter’s wife. Peter had a mother-in-law, so he was married; Paul later mentions that Peter took his wife with him on his travels (1 Corinthians 9:5). Protestant and Orthodox churches allow married clergy. The Catholic Church in the West normally requires priests to be celibate as a matter of discipline (not doctrine), while in its Eastern churches ‘married men can be ordained as deacons and priests’ (Catechism 1579–1580).

1.ctx: After a day of crowds and healing, the whole town wanted more.
1.mean: ‘Early in the morning, while it was still dark, Jesus got up and went out to a solitary place to pray.’ Simon and the others hunt him down: ‘Everyone is looking for You!’ But Jesus will not be held by popularity: ‘Let us go on to the neighboring towns so I can preach there as well, for that is why I have come.’ So he goes throughout Galilee, preaching and driving out demons.
1.big: Jesus’ priorities came from time alone with his Father, not from the demands of the crowd.

1.ctx: ‘Leprosy’ in the Bible covers various skin diseases (BSB footnote). Under Leviticus 13 a sufferer was unclean, had to live apart and warn others away. Touching him made a person unclean.
1.mean: A leper kneels: ‘If You are willing, You can make me clean.’ He has no doubt about Jesus’ power, only his willingness. ‘Moved with compassion, Jesus reached out His hand and touched the man. “I am willing,” He said. “Be clean!”’ Instead of Jesus becoming unclean, the leper becomes clean. Jesus sends him to the priest to make the offering Moses commanded, so that he can be officially restored to the community, and sternly tells him to say nothing. The man tells everyone, and Jesus can no longer enter towns openly.
1.big: Jesus is both able and willing, and his touch reverses contamination: holiness flows outward from him.
1.diff: A textual question. Some ancient manuscripts read ‘Moved with indignation’ instead of ‘compassion’ (BSB footnote). If original, it may be anger at the disease and its effects rather than at the man. Either way, Jesus touches him.

hist.t: Why did Jesus tell people to keep quiet? (the ‘Messianic secret’)
b: Again and again in Mark, Jesus tells demons, people he has healed and even his disciples not to make him known (1:34, 44; 3:12; 5:43; 8:30; 9:9). In 1901 the German scholar William Wrede argued that Jesus never claimed to be the Messiah, and that Mark (or his sources) invented these commands to explain why Jesus had not been recognised as Messiah during his life.

Many scholars since have rejected Wrede’s theory: Mark is full of open claims and actions too, and the secrecy is not consistent enough to be a cover story. Most now see historical reasons for it. ‘Messiah’ and ‘Son of God’ carried political overtones; Roman governors executed would-be kings, and crowds could turn a healer into a rebel leader (compare John 6:15). Jesus also needed to redefine what kind of Messiah he was, one who must suffer (8:31), before the title could be safely used. After the resurrection the secret is to be told (9:9).

2.ctx: Houses in Capernaum were built of local basalt with flat roofs of wooden beams, branches and packed earth, reached by an outside stair.
2.mean: The house is packed, so four men dig through the roof and lower their paralysed friend on his mat. ‘When Jesus saw their faith, He said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven.”’ The scribes are scandalised: ‘He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?’ Their theology is correct. Jesus asks which is easier to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven’ or ‘Get up’. Anyone can say the first, since no one can check it. So ‘that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins’, he heals the man, who walks out in front of them all.
2.big: Jesus claims to do what only God can do, and proves it with something everyone can see.

2.ctx: Tax collectors bought the right to collect tolls for Herod Antipas or for Rome and kept what they could make above that. They were seen as collaborators and cheats; respectable Jews would not eat with them.
2.mean: Jesus sees Levi son of Alphaeus at his tax booth and says, ‘Follow Me’, and Levi follows (Matthew’s Gospel calls him Matthew, 9:9). At a dinner in Levi’s house many ‘tax collectors and sinners’ eat with Jesus. The scribes of the Pharisees object. Jesus replies: ‘It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.’
2.big: Jesus seeks out the people religious society wrote off; only those who know they are sick come to the doctor.

2.ctx: The Law required fasting only on the Day of Atonement, but devout Pharisees fasted twice a week (Luke 18:12). John’s disciples fasted too.
2.mean: People ask why Jesus’ disciples do not fast. He answers with a wedding picture: ‘How can the guests of the bridegroom fast while He is with them?’ A wedding was a week of celebration. In the prophets God is Israel’s husband (Hosea 2:16), so Jesus is quietly casting himself in God’s role. ‘But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast’, the first hint in Mark of his violent death.
2.big: Jesus’ presence is a time for joy; his followers would fast after he was taken away.

2.ctx: New cloth shrinks when washed; new wine ferments and expands. Old leather wineskins had lost their stretch.
2.mean: Two little parables. A patch of unshrunk cloth will tear an old garment; new wine will burst old wineskins. ‘Instead, new wine is poured into new wineskins.’ What Jesus brings cannot simply be stitched onto existing religious practice as an extra. It needs new forms.
2.big: The kingdom Jesus brings is not a patch on the old system but something new.

2.ctx: Picking grain by hand from a neighbour’s field was allowed (Deuteronomy 23:25), but the Pharisees counted it as harvesting, forbidden on the Sabbath.
2.mean: The Pharisees challenge Jesus over his disciples picking grain. He points to David, who, hungry and on the run, ate the consecrated bread that only priests could eat (1 Samuel 21). Then two great statements: ‘The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. Therefore, the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.’ God gave the Sabbath as a gift for human good, and Jesus claims authority over the day God himself instituted.
2.big: The Sabbath is God’s gift, and Jesus is its Lord.
2.diff: ‘Abiathar’. First Samuel 21 names the priest as Ahimelech, Abiathar’s father. Abiathar was there, escaped Saul’s massacre, and became David’s high priest. The New Bible Dictionary notes that the Greek phrase can be rendered ‘in the passage about Abiathar’, the way Jesus refers to Exodus 3 as ‘the burning bush’ (12:26). Christians and the Sabbath. The Reformed tradition holds that the Sabbath command still binds, and that since the resurrection it is kept on the first day as ‘the Christian Sabbath’ (Westminster Confession 21.7–8). Lutherans hold that the gospel has set aside the Sabbath ceremony, and that the church chose Sunday so that people would know when to meet (Augsburg Confession 28). Catholic teaching says Sunday ‘fulfills the spiritual truth of the Jewish sabbath’ (Catechism 2175). Seventh-day Adventists keep Saturday.

3.ctx: Rabbis allowed healing on the Sabbath only if life was in danger. A withered hand was not urgent; it could wait a day.
3.mean: In the synagogue his opponents watch to see if he will heal on the Sabbath, ‘In order to accuse Jesus’. He calls the man to stand in front of everyone and asks: ‘Which is lawful on the Sabbath: to do good or to do evil, to save life or to destroy it?’ They are silent. ‘Jesus looked around at them with anger and sorrow at their hardness of heart.’ He heals the hand with a word, doing no ‘work’ at all. And the Pharisees go out to plot with the Herodians how to kill him: on the Sabbath, they plan to destroy life.
3.big: Refusing to do good is itself a choice for evil; and Jesus’ anger at hard hearts is mixed with grief.

b: The Herodians appear only in the Gospels (here, 12:13 and Matthew 22:16), and no ancient source describes them fully. They were apparently Jews who supported the rule of Herod’s family, and so, indirectly, Rome. Pharisees and Herodians normally had little in common; that they joined forces against Jesus shows how threatening both groups found him.

src.l: ‘Herodians’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

3.ctx: Idumea was far to the south, and Tyre and Sidon were Gentile cities on the coast to the north-west. People were coming from every direction.
3.mean: Huge crowds come from all over the region. Jesus has a boat ready so they will not crush him, ‘For He had healed so many that all who had diseases were pressing forward to touch Him.’ Unclean spirits fall down and cry ‘You are the Son of God!’, but Jesus sternly orders them not to make him known.
3.big: Jesus did not accept testimony to himself from demons; he would make himself known in his own way and time.

3.ctx: Israel had twelve tribes. Choosing twelve signalled that Jesus was reconstituting God’s people around himself.
3.mean: On a mountain Jesus calls ‘those He wanted’ and appoints twelve: first ‘to accompany Him’, then ‘to be sent out to preach, and to have authority to drive out demons.’ Being with him comes before being sent. The list is a strange mixture: fishermen; a tax collector (Matthew); ‘Simon the Zealot’, whose name may mean he had been an anti-Roman nationalist; and ‘Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus’. Simon is renamed Peter (‘Rock’) and James and John ‘Sons of Thunder’.
3.big: Jesus chooses unlikely people, wants them first to be with him, and then sends them out.

3.ctx: ‘Beelzebul’ (‘lord of the house’) was a name for the prince of demons. The scribes ‘from Jerusalem’ were an official delegation.
3.mean: Jesus’ family come to ‘take custody of Him, saying, “He is out of His mind.”’ The Jerusalem scribes have a worse explanation: ‘He is possessed by Beelzebul’. Jesus shows the absurdity: ‘How can Satan drive out Satan?’ A kingdom or house divided against itself cannot stand. Rather, ‘no one can enter a strong man’s house to steal his possessions unless he first ties up the strong man.’ Satan is the strong man; Jesus is the stronger one who has come to bind him and set his captives free.
3.big: Jesus’ exorcisms are not Satan’s tricks but Satan’s defeat.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Mark 3:23–30 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

3.ctx: This saying follows directly on the scribes’ claim that Jesus’ work by the Spirit was the devil’s work.
3.mean: ‘Truly I tell you, the sons of men will be forgiven all sins and blasphemies, as many as they utter.’ The generosity is staggering. ‘But whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit will never be forgiven; he is guilty of eternal sin.’ Mark explains why Jesus said it: ‘because they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit.”’ The scribes saw God’s Spirit plainly at work and called it Satan.
3.big: Every sin can be forgiven, except the settled refusal that calls God’s saving work evil and so shuts the door on the only source of forgiveness.
3.diff: Christians broadly agree that this is not a careless word or a single sin a believer might commit by accident. Calvin says those who reject the Spirit’s work ‘after that the power of God has been revealed, cannot be excused on the plea of ignorance’. Wesley defined it as ‘ascribing those miracles to the power of the devil which Christ wrought by the power of the Holy Ghost’. Pastors in every tradition add that a person anxious about having committed it shows by that very anxiety that they have not.

3.ctx: This picks up the story from 3:21, where Jesus’ family set out to take him home.
3.mean: Jesus’ mother and brothers arrive and send for him. Looking at the people sitting around him, he says, ‘Here are My mother and My brothers! For whoever does the will of God is My brother and sister and mother.’ He is not disowning his family (compare John 19:26–27), but he is defining a new family, bound together by doing God’s will.
3.big: Jesus’ followers become his family, closer even than blood.
3.diff: Who Jesus’ ‘brothers’ were is discussed at 6:1. Wesley noted that ‘neither did these of his brethren believe on him’ at this time (John 7:5), though James later became a leader in the church.

4.ctx: A parable is a short story from everyday life that carries a spiritual meaning. In Palestine seed was often scattered by hand and then ploughed in, so some inevitably fell on paths and stony patches.
4.mean: Teaching from a boat, Jesus tells of a farmer whose seed falls in four places: on the path, where birds eat it; on rocky ground, where it springs up and withers; among thorns, which choke it; and on good soil, where it yields ‘thirtyfold, another sixtyfold, and another a hundredfold’. A good harvest was perhaps sevenfold to tenfold; these are extraordinary yields. ‘He who has ears to hear, let him hear.’
4.big: Much of the sowing seems wasted, but the harvest will be astonishing.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Mark 4:1–12 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

4.ctx: Verse 12 quotes Isaiah 6:9–10, where Isaiah is warned that his preaching will harden a stubborn people.
4.mean: Alone with the Twelve and others, Jesus says: ‘The mystery of the kingdom of God has been given to you, but to those on the outside everything is expressed in parables, so that, ‘they may be ever seeing but never perceiving, and ever hearing but never understanding; otherwise they might turn and be forgiven.’’ Parables reveal and conceal at the same time. To those who come close and ask, they open up; to those who stay outside, they remain riddles.
4.big: The same word that opens the eyes of seekers leaves the indifferent more blind.
4.diff: Does God harden people? Reformed theology takes this as God’s judicial hardening: Calvin says the word ‘blinds and hardens the reprobate’, yet ‘through their own depravity’, as weak eyes are dazzled by the sun. Arminian (Wesleyan) theology stresses that the hardening follows human choice: Wesley wrote, ‘They would not see before now they could not, God having given them up to the blindness which they had chosen.’ Both agree that the hardened are responsible, and that the purpose of preaching is that people ‘might turn and be forgiven’.

4.h: The Parable of the Sower Explained
4.ctx: This is one of the few parables Jesus explains point by point, giving a key for reading the others.
4.mean: ‘The farmer sows the word.’ The path is those from whom ‘Satan comes and takes away the word’. The rocky ground is those who receive it ‘with joy’ but have no root, and when trouble or persecution comes ‘they quickly fall away’. The thorns are those in whom ‘the worries of this life, the deceitfulness of wealth, and the desire for other things’ choke the word. The good soil is those who ‘hear the word, receive it, and produce a crop’.
4.big: What matters is not a quick, joyful start but lasting fruit; and the threats are Satan, suffering and the cares and riches of life.
4.diff: Rocky ground and falling away. Reformed readers take the rocky and thorny soils as people who never truly had saving faith, however promising their start, since true faith perseveres. Arminian (Wesleyan) readers see real believers who can lose what they had. Both treat the parable as a warning to keep hearing and bearing fruit.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Mark 4:1–12 (trans. Pringle), CCEL

4.ctx: A small clay oil lamp was the only light in a one-room house. A ‘basket’ was a measuring bowl for grain.
4.mean: Nobody lights a lamp to hide it. ‘For there is nothing hidden that will not be disclosed’: the kingdom, now partly hidden in parables, will one day be fully seen. Then a warning about listening: ‘With the measure you use, it will be measured to you’. ‘For whoever has will be given more. But whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken away from him.’
4.big: Those who listen carefully receive more; those who ignore what they have heard lose even that.

4.ctx: This parable is found only in Mark.
4.mean: ‘The kingdom of God is like a man who scatters seed on the ground.’ He sleeps and wakes, ‘and the seed sprouts and grows, though he knows not how. All by itself the earth produces a crop’. When the grain is ripe, he puts in the sickle, ‘because the harvest has come’ (echoing Joel 3:13).
4.big: The sower sows, but God gives the growth, quietly, steadily and beyond our understanding, until the harvest.
4.diff: Christians of every tradition find encouragement here for evangelism and patience. Wesley, typically, also stressed human effort alongside God’s: the earth brings forth no corn ‘without both the care and toil of man’. Calvin stressed that the growth is God’s alone.

src.l: John Wesley, Explanatory Notes on Mark 4

4.h: The Parable of the Mustard Seed
4.ctx: The black mustard seed was proverbially the tiniest seed. The plant can grow to around three metres in a season.
4.mean: The kingdom of God ‘is like a mustard seed, which is the smallest of all seeds sown upon the earth’, but grows into ‘the largest of all garden plants’, so big that ‘the birds of the air nest in its shade’, an image the prophets used for a great kingdom sheltering the nations (Ezekiel 17:23; Daniel 4:12). Mark adds that Jesus taught many such parables ‘to the extent that they could understand’, and explained everything privately to his disciples.
4.big: From a Galilean teacher and twelve followers, the kingdom of God will grow beyond all expectation.
4.diff: ‘The smallest of all seeds’. Botanically, some seeds (such as orchid seeds) are smaller. Jesus is using the proverbial smallest seed known to his hearers, in the way people still speak of something as small as a mustard seed, not giving a botanical ranking.

4.ctx: The Sea of Galilee lies about 210 m below sea level, surrounded by hills. Cold air can funnel down the valleys and raise sudden violent storms.
4.mean: Crossing at evening, they are caught in a ‘violent windstorm’, and the boat is being swamped. Jesus is asleep in the stern on a cushion, fully human and exhausted. They wake him: ‘Teacher, don’t You care that we are perishing?’ He rebukes the wind and says to the sea, ‘Silence!’ and ‘Be still!’, and ‘it was perfectly calm.’ Then: ‘Why are you so afraid?’ … ‘Do you still have no faith?’ Now they are more afraid than before: ‘Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?’
4.big: The one asleep in the boat is the Lord who stills the sea (Psalm 107:28–29), and his presence is the answer to fear.

5.ctx: The east side of the lake was largely Gentile territory, part of the Decapolis (‘Ten Cities’). Jews regarded pigs, tombs and demons as unclean; this man was surrounded by all three.
5.mean: A man with an unclean spirit lives among the tombs, too strong to be chained, ‘crying out and cutting himself with stones’. He runs and falls before Jesus: ‘What do You want with me, Jesus, Son of the Most High God?’ Asked his name, he says, ‘My name is Legion,’ ‘for we are many.’ (A Roman legion was some 5,000 soldiers.) The demons beg to be sent into a herd of about two thousand pigs, which rush into the sea and drown. The townspeople come and find the man ‘sitting there, clothed and in his right mind; and they were afraid.’ They beg Jesus to leave. The man asks to go with him, but Jesus sends him home: ‘tell them how much the Lord has done for you’. He proclaims ‘how much Jesus had done for him’ throughout the Decapolis.
5.big: No one is too far gone for Jesus; and the first missionary to the Gentile Decapolis is a man who had been possessed by a legion.
5.diff: The pigs. Readers have long asked why Jesus allowed the loss of the herd. Calvin admits ‘the reason of it is not known by us with certainty’, but suggests the demons aimed ‘to excite the inhabitants of that country to curse God on account of the loss of the swine’. He adds that the event shows demons are real spirits, not just human vices. Others note that it showed the man, visibly, that his tormentors had really gone, and that one human life is worth more than many animals.

b: Mark’s earliest manuscripts say ‘the region of the Gerasenes’; others read Gadarenes or Gergesenes (BSB footnote), and Matthew’s best manuscripts say Gadarenes (Matthew 8:28). The ancient copyists were already wrestling with the geography.

Gerasa (modern Jerash, in Jordan) was a famous city, but about 55 km from the lake, too far for the pigs to rush into the sea. Gadara (Umm Qais) was about 10 km south-east of the lake and controlled land down to the shore. Gergesa, at modern el-Kursi on the east shore, has steep slopes near the water and ancient caves that could have been tombs; Origen (3rd century) proposed it.

A common solution is that Mark and Luke name the wider district by its best-known city, and Matthew by the nearer city that owned the land; ‘region of’ is a broad term. The incident itself fits the east shore, Gentile country with pig herds, and Kursi is the site most often suggested. The exact spot cannot be fixed.

5.ctx: A synagogue leader was a respected lay official. A woman with continual bleeding was ritually unclean (Leviticus 15:25) and anyone she touched became unclean, so she would have been excluded from much of normal life.
5.mean: Jairus falls at Jesus’ feet: his little daughter is dying. On the way a woman who has bled for twelve years, impoverished by doctors, touches Jesus’ cloak from behind and is healed at once. Jesus stops: ‘Who touched My garments?’ She comes forward trembling and tells him everything. ‘Daughter,’ he says, ‘your faith has healed you. Go in peace and be free of your affliction.’ He restores her publicly, not just physically. Meanwhile news comes that Jairus’s daughter is dead. Jesus says, ‘Do not be afraid; just believe.’ At the house the mourners laugh at him for saying, ‘The child is not dead, but asleep.’ He takes her hand: ‘Talitha koum!’, which means ‘Little girl, I say to you, get up!’, and she gets up and walks. He tells them to give her something to eat.
5.big: Jesus has time for the outcast and power over death; for him, death is like sleep from which he wakes people.
5.diff: ‘Your faith has healed you’. Jesus credits faith, but the power is his (verse 30), and her faith was weak and partly superstitious. Christians have always prayed for healing; they differ on how far healing should be expected today. Pentecostals such as the Assemblies of God teach that deliverance from sickness ‘is provided for in the Atonement, and is the privilege of all believers’, while admitting, ‘We do not understand fully why some are healed and others are not.’ Most other traditions pray for healing while accepting that God does not always grant it in this life (compare 2 Corinthians 12:7–9). The story of the twelve-year-old girl and the twelve-year illness interweave deliberately: Jesus is never too late.

src.l: Assemblies of God, ‘Divine Healing’ (position paper, quoting the Statement of Fundamental Truths, sec. 12)

6.ctx: Nazareth, Jesus’ home town, was a small village where everyone knew his family.
6.mean: Jesus teaches in his home synagogue, and the people are astonished: ‘Where did this man get these ideas?’ But astonishment turns to offence: ‘Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary and the brother of James, Joses, Judas, and Simon? Aren’t His sisters here with us as well?’ They knew him too well to believe in him. Jesus replies, ‘Only in his hometown, among his relatives, and in his own household is a prophet without honor.’ ‘So He could not perform any miracles there, except to lay His hands on a few of the sick and heal them. And He was amazed at their unbelief.’
6.big: Familiarity with Jesus’ ordinary life became, for his own town, a reason not to believe.
6.diff: ‘Could not’. This does not mean Jesus’ power failed. In Mark, miracles are not shows to force belief (8:11–12); where people refuse to trust him, he does not impose them. Who were Jesus’ brothers and sisters? Christians hold three views. Most Protestants today take them as younger children of Mary and Joseph, the plainest reading of the words (the view of Helvidius in the 4th century). Orthodox tradition (following Epiphanius) holds they were Joseph’s children by an earlier marriage. Catholic teaching (following Jerome) holds they were close relatives; the Catechism says James and Joseph are ‘the sons of another Mary’ (500; compare 15:40). The Reformers did not take the first view: Calvin said Helvidius ‘displayed excessive ignorance in concluding that Mary must have had many sons’, since ‘brothers’ in Hebrew usage can mean relatives; and Wesley wrote that Mary ‘as well after as before she brought Him forth, continued a pure and unspotted virgin’. The Greek word can mean relatives, but its normal sense is brothers, and Mark lists them with their mother. Nothing in the gospel depends on the answer.

b: Nazareth was a small Jewish farming village on a ridge in Lower Galilee: current estimates suggest 200–500 people in Jesus’ day. No writer before the New Testament mentions it, not even Josephus, which fits a place of no importance (compare John 1:46). Excavations under the Church of the Annunciation found silos, cisterns, tombs and simple houses.

About 6 km away stood Sepphoris, which Herod Antipas rebuilt as his capital after 4 BC. The word translated ‘carpenter’ (Greek tektōn) means a builder or craftsman in wood or stone. Building work at Sepphoris would have drawn craftsmen from the surrounding villages, and many scholars think Joseph and Jesus may have worked there, though the Gospels never mention it.

6.ctx: Travelling teachers depended on hospitality. Shaking dust off the feet was what devout Jews did on leaving Gentile land: a sign of separation.
6.mean: Jesus sends the Twelve out ‘two by two, giving them authority over unclean spirits.’ They are to take ‘nothing but a staff for the journey—no bread, no bag, no money in their belts’, trusting God and their hosts. If a place will not listen, they are to ‘shake the dust off your feet when you leave that place, as a testimony against them.’ ‘So they set out and preached that the people should repent. They also drove out many demons and healed many of the sick, anointing them with oil.’
6.big: Jesus shares his mission and his authority with his followers, and sends them out dependent on God.
6.diff: Anointing with oil. Oil was used as medicine and as a sign of God’s blessing. Catholic and Orthodox churches see here, and in James 5:14–15, the roots of the sacrament of anointing the sick: the Catholic Catechism says it ‘is alluded to indeed by Mark, but is recommended to the faithful and promulgated by James’ (1511). Calvin saw the anointing as ‘a visible token of spiritual grace’ that went with the apostles’ gift of healing, given ‘as a temporary seal of the doctrine of the Gospel’. Many Protestant churches still anoint the sick with prayer, following James 5, without calling it a sacrament.

6.ctx: Mark tells this story in a flashback while the Twelve are away. Leviticus 18:16 and 20:21 forbade marrying a brother’s wife while he was alive.
6.mean: Herod hears about Jesus, and his guilty conscience speaks: ‘John, whom I beheaded, has risen from the dead!’ Mark explains. Herod had married Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, and John had told him, ‘It is not lawful for you to have your brother’s wife!’ Herodias wanted John dead, but Herod ‘feared John and protected him, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man’, and liked to listen to him. At his birthday banquet, Herodias’s daughter dances, and Herod rashly swears to give her anything, ‘up to half my kingdom!’ Prompted by her mother she asks for ‘the head of John the Baptist on a platter’. ‘The king was consumed with sorrow’, but to save face before his guests, he gives the order. John’s disciples bury his body.
6.big: A weak man who knew what was right chose to save face; and the forerunner’s death foreshadows what awaits Jesus.

hist.t: Herod Antipas, Herodias and John’s death
b: The ‘King Herod’ of Mark 6 is Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great. After his father died in 4 BC, Augustus made him tetrarch (ruler of a quarter) of Galilee and Perea, which he governed for 43 years. Matthew and Luke give his exact title, ‘tetrarch’; Mark uses the popular ‘king’. He rebuilt Sepphoris and founded Tiberias on the Sea of Galilee.

Josephus confirms the outline of Mark’s account. Antipas divorced his first wife, daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas, to marry Herodias, who had been married to his half-brother. Josephus calls that first husband Herod; Mark calls him Philip. Since several of Herod the Great’s sons were called Herod, some suggest he bore both names. Aretas later defeated Antipas in battle, and Josephus says many Jews saw the defeat as God’s punishment for his killing of ‘John, that was called the Baptist’, ‘a good man’ who called the Jews to righteousness and baptism.

Josephus gives a political reason for the execution: Antipas feared John’s influence over the crowds might lead to a revolt. Mark gives the personal story. The two fit together easily. Josephus says John was held and killed at Machaerus, Antipas’s fortress east of the Dead Sea.

6.h: The Feeding of the Five Thousand
6.ctx: This is the only miracle (apart from the resurrection) told in all four Gospels. A denarius was a day’s wage; two hundred denarii was most of a year’s pay.
6.mean: The apostles return and Jesus takes them away to rest, but the crowds get there first. ‘He had compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd’, and he teaches them. When it grows late, the disciples want to send people away; Jesus says, ‘You give them something to eat.’ They have ‘Five—and two fish.’ He seats the people in groups on the green grass, looks up to heaven, blesses and breaks the loaves, and gives them to the disciples to distribute. ‘They all ate and were satisfied’, and twelve baskets of leftovers are collected. ‘And there were five thousand men who had eaten the loaves.’
6.big: Jesus is the shepherd Israel lacked (Ezekiel 34), who feeds his people in the wilderness as God fed them with manna.
6.diff: Some modern writers have explained the miracle as people being moved to share food they had hidden. The Gospels give no hint of this; all four present it as a miracle of multiplication, and the disciples’ failure to understand it (6:52; 8:17–21) would make no sense otherwise. The actions ‘took…blessed…broke…gave’ anticipate the Last Supper (14:22).

6.ctx: The ‘fourth watch’ was 3–6 a.m. (BSB footnote). In the Old Testament, God alone ‘treads on the waves of the sea’ (Job 9:8).
6.mean: Jesus sends the disciples ahead by boat and goes up the mountain to pray. In the night he sees them ‘straining to row, because the wind was against them’, and comes to them, ‘walking on the sea. He intended to pass by them’, language that echoes God ‘passing by’ Moses and Elijah to reveal his glory (Exodus 33:19–22; 1 Kings 19:11). They think he is a ghost. ‘Take courage! It is I. Do not be afraid.’ (‘It is I’ is literally ‘I am’, echoing God’s name.) He gets in and the wind stops. They are astounded, ‘for they had not understood about the loaves, but their hearts had been hardened.’
6.big: Jesus does what only God does and speaks as God speaks; yet even his closest followers were slow to understand.

6.ctx: Gennesaret was a fertile plain on the north-west shore of the lake, south of Capernaum. The ‘fringe’ was probably the tassel that devout Jews wore on their cloaks (Numbers 15:38–39).
6.mean: As soon as they land, people recognise Jesus and run through the region carrying the sick to wherever he is. In villages, towns and countryside they lay them in the marketplaces and beg ‘just to let them touch the fringe of His cloak. And all who touched Him were healed.’
6.big: Where people come to Jesus with their need, he does not turn them away.

7.ctx: The ‘tradition of the elders’ was an oral body of rules that Pharisees believed went back to Moses, later written down in the Mishnah. Hand-washing before meals was a ritual purity custom extended from priests to everyone, not a matter of hygiene. ‘Corban’ meant a gift dedicated to God.
7.mean: Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem see Jesus’ disciples eating with unwashed hands and ask why they ignore the tradition of the elders. Jesus answers with Isaiah 29:13: ‘These people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me.’ ‘You have disregarded the commandment of God to keep the tradition of men.’ His example: God commanded, ‘Honor your father and your mother’, but their rules let a son declare his money ‘Corban’, devoted to God, and so refuse to support his parents. ‘Thus you nullify the word of God by the tradition you have handed down.’
7.big: Religious rules can become a way of avoiding what God actually commands.
7.diff: Scripture and tradition. Protestants read this passage as a warning that all church traditions must be tested by Scripture, the only infallible rule (Westminster Confession 1.6, 1.10). Calvin drew the principle that ‘all kinds of worship invented by men are of no estimation in his sight’. Catholic and Orthodox Christians agree that merely human traditions can contradict God’s word, but distinguish them from apostolic Tradition, which hands on what the apostles received and which they hold together with Scripture as one deposit of revelation. The Catholic Catechism distinguishes that Tradition from ‘the various theological, disciplinary, liturgical or devotional traditions, born in the local churches over time’ (80–83). All agree that no tradition may be used to cancel a plain command of God, as the Corban rule did.

src.l: Calvin, Harmony of the Evangelists, on Mark 7:1–13 (trans. Pringle), CCEL
Westminster Confession of Faith (OPC text)
Catechism of the Catholic Church 80–83 (Tradition and Scripture)

7.ctx: The food laws of Leviticus 11 marked Israel out from the nations. Whether Gentile Christians had to keep them became a burning issue in the early church (Acts 10; 15; Romans 14).
7.mean: Jesus calls the crowd: ‘Nothing that enters a man from the outside can defile him; but the things that come out of a man, these are what defile him.’ Food goes into the stomach, not the heart. Mark adds his own comment: ‘(Thus all foods are clean.)’ What defiles is what comes out of the heart: ‘evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, greed, wickedness, deceit, debauchery, envy, slander, arrogance, and foolishness.’
7.big: Our real problem is not outside us but inside; and Christ’s coming ends the food laws that once marked Israel off.
7.diff: Almost all churches read Mark’s comment as declaring the Old Testament food laws fulfilled and no longer binding (compare Acts 10:15; Romans 14:14). Seventh-day Adventists hold that the distinction between clean and unclean meats still applies as a matter of health. The BSB footnote gives an alternative translation of verse 19 that applies the words to digestion, but most translations follow the reading in the text.

src.l: Seventh-day Adventist Church, 28 Fundamental Beliefs, no. 22 ‘Christian Behavior’

7.h: The Faith of the Gentile Woman
7.ctx: Tyre was a wealthy Gentile city on the coast, north-west of Galilee. Jews sometimes called Gentiles ‘dogs’; the word Jesus uses here can mean little dogs or house dogs (BSB footnote: ‘puppies’).
7.mean: Jesus goes into Gentile territory and tries to stay hidden. A Greek woman of Syrophoenician origin falls at his feet and begs him to free her daughter from a demon. ‘First let the children have their fill,’ he says. ‘For it is not right to take the children’s bread and toss it to the dogs.’ Israel comes first in God’s plan. She does not argue but takes his words and turns them: ‘Yes, Lord,’ ‘even the dogs under the table eat the children’s crumbs.’ ‘Because of this answer, you may go. The demon has left your daughter.’ She goes home and finds it so.
7.big: God’s blessing came to Israel first, but a Gentile mother’s humble, persistent faith shows it was always meant for the nations too.

7.ctx: The Decapolis, south-east of the lake, was again Gentile territory. Mark keeps Jesus’ Aramaic word, as at 5:41.
7.mean: People bring a deaf man who can hardly speak. Jesus takes him aside, puts his fingers in his ears, spits and touches his tongue, using touch to communicate with a man who cannot hear. He looks up to heaven, sighs, and says ‘Ephphatha!’ (‘Be opened!’). The man hears and speaks plainly. The crowd say, ‘He has done all things well! He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak!’, echoing Isaiah 35:5–6, the promise of what God would do when he came to save.
7.big: Jesus does the works Isaiah said would mark God’s coming, and he deals with each person in a way they can understand.

8.h: The Feeding of the Four Thousand
8.ctx: This second feeding takes place in the largely Gentile region of the Decapolis (7:31). Dalmanutha (verse 10) is otherwise unknown; it was somewhere on the western shore.
8.mean: Another large crowd has been with Jesus three days with nothing to eat. ‘I have compassion for this crowd’, he says. The disciples ask, ‘Where in this desolate place could anyone find enough bread to feed all these people?’, as though the first feeding had never happened. With seven loaves and a few fish he feeds about four thousand, and seven basketfuls are left.
8.big: Jesus’ compassion and provision reach Gentiles as well as Jews.
8.diff: Some scholars think the two feedings are two versions of one event. Mark clearly regards them as two (8:19–20), with different numbers, places and words for ‘basket’. Many see significance in the settings: twelve baskets among Jews, seven among Gentiles.

src.l: ‘Magdala’, Lexham Bible Dictionary

8.ctx: A ‘sign from heaven’ meant some spectacular proof directly from God, beyond the healings they had already seen.
8.mean: Pharisees come and demand ‘a sign from heaven’, to test him. ‘Jesus sighed deeply in His spirit and said, “Why does this generation demand a sign? Truly I tell you, no sign will be given to this generation.”’ He leaves them.
8.big: Jesus does not perform on demand for people who have already decided not to believe.

8.h: The Leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod
8.ctx: Leaven (yeast) works its way invisibly through a whole batch of dough; it was a common picture of a spreading corrupt influence.
8.mean: In the boat with one loaf, Jesus warns, ‘Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod.’ The disciples think he is talking about bread. He asks a string of searching questions: ‘Do you still not see or understand? Do you have such hard hearts?’ He reminds them of the twelve and the seven baskets. ‘Do you still not understand?’
8.big: Unbelief can be catching; and even disciples can be slow to see what is in front of them.

8.ctx: This healing, found only in Mark, comes right after Jesus rebukes the disciples for having eyes and not seeing (8:18).
8.mean: At Bethsaida Jesus leads a blind man out of the village, spits on his eyes, lays hands on him and asks, ‘Can you see anything?’ ‘I can see the people, but they look like trees walking around.’ Jesus lays hands on him again, ‘and he could see everything clearly.’
8.big: A two-stage healing, placed where Mark puts it, pictures the disciples: they see something of Jesus, but not yet clearly.
8.diff: Some ask whether the first touch ‘failed’. The Gospel does not suggest Jesus was struggling. Most commentators see an acted parable: in the next scene Peter sees that Jesus is the Christ, but blurrily, because he cannot accept a suffering Christ.

b: Bethsaida (‘house of fishing’) was the home town of Peter, Andrew and Philip (John 1:44). Josephus says that Philip the tetrarch, another son of Herod the Great, enlarged the village and renamed it Julias, in honour of the emperor Augustus’s daughter.

Two sites near the north shore of the lake are proposed. Et-Tell, about 2.5 km inland, has been excavated continuously since 1987 by Rami Arav and Richard Freund. It has impressive Iron Age remains (Arav suggests it was the capital of the Old Testament kingdom of Geshur, 2 Samuel 15:8) and a Roman-period settlement, including a building some excavators identify as a small Roman temple. Critics such as Jodi Magness say its Roman remains are too modest for the town Josephus describes. El-Araj, on the shore, was long thought to have only later remains, but excavations led by Steven Notley and Mordechai Aviam since 2016 have reported a Roman-era bathhouse (1st–3rd centuries AD) and a later Byzantine church. Arav replies that there is not yet evidence of an earlier Jewish fishing village there. Scholars are divided.

8.ctx: This is the turning point of Mark. Caesarea Philippi lay at the foot of Mount Hermon, 40 km north of the lake, a city full of pagan worship.
8.mean: On the road Jesus asks, ‘Who do people say I am?’ They report the popular views: John the Baptist, Elijah, one of the prophets. ‘But what about you?’ Jesus asked. ‘Who do you say I am?’ Peter answers, ‘You are the Christ.’ Jesus warns them not to tell anyone, because the word ‘Christ’ (Messiah) meant to most people a conquering king, and he must first teach them what kind of Christ he is.
8.big: Everything turns on the question every reader must answer: ‘Who do you say I am?’
8.diff: Peter and the ‘rock’. Mark, traditionally Peter’s Gospel, records only Peter’s confession. Matthew adds Jesus’ reply, ‘on this rock I will build My church’ and the keys (Matthew 16:18–19). Catholic teaching holds that the Church is ‘built on Peter’, who received ‘a unique mission’ that continues in his successors, the bishops of Rome (Catechism 552–553). Orthodox tradition honours Peter’s primacy among the apostles but does not accept the papacy’s claims of jurisdiction. Most Protestants follow Calvin in taking the rock to be Peter as confessor of Christ, or the faith he confessed, which is ‘the common foundation of the whole Church’. See the note on Matthew 16.

hist.t: Caesarea Philippi and the shrine of Pan
b: The city stood beside a large cave from which one of the sources of the Jordan flowed. In the Greek period the cave became a shrine to the god Pan, and the place was called Panias (the modern name is still Banias). About 20 BC the emperor Augustus gave the area to Herod the Great, who built a white marble temple to Augustus there, according to Josephus. Herod’s son Philip developed the town into a city and named it Caesarea in honour of the emperor, adding his own name to distinguish it from Caesarea on the coast.
The cave can still be seen at Banias. Many preachers draw out the setting: among shrines to Pan and to a deified emperor, Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ.
